source_text: Ad moralem locum: habes et tu vitulum — carnem superbum. Si munus Domino offerre vis, adduc ad ostium tabernaculi — auditum divinorum librorum. Masculinum sit munus; impone manum et iugula contra Dominum — continentiae frenum, macero corpus meum. Filii Aaron in te — mens et sensus — offerant sanguinem. Hostiam vivam, sanctam, placentem Deo. Completur Homilia I. Amen.
thought_title: The moral application of the calf offering
orientation: Origen turns from the spiritual sense of the calf to the moral sense, addressing the hearer directly about offering one's own flesh as a living sacrifice.
pass_a_gloss: To the moral place: you also have a calf — proud flesh. If you wish to offer a gift to the Lord, lead it to the door of the tabernacle — the hearing of the divine books. Let the gift be male; place the hand and cut the throat before the Lord — the bridle of self-control, I bruise my body. The sons of Aaron in you — mind and sense — let them offer the blood. A living victim, holy, pleasing to God. Homily I is completed. Amen.

choices.why: Keeps the literal fleshly sense and the moral vice of pride together, matching Origen's move from the calf to the hearer's own body.

choices.english: lead it to the door of the tabernacle
choices.why: Preserves the command form and the spatial movement of the Levitical rite, which Origen immediately reinterprets as hearing Scripture.
rejected: bring it to the entrance of the tent
present it at the tabernacle door

choices.english: the hearing of the divine books
choices.why: Keeps the genitive construction and the sense of attentive listening to Scripture as the moral equivalent of the tabernacle door.
Renders frenum as bridle to keep the image of restraint, and continentiae as self-control per the moral sense of the passage.
Echoes the Pauline language of bodily discipline and keeps the first-person present force of the verb.
Keeps hostia as victim to preserve the sacrificial force, and vivam as living to mark the contrast with the slain calf.

pass_b_english: Now turn to the moral sense. You too have a calf—your proud flesh. If you wish to offer a gift to the Lord, lead it to the door of the tabernacle, which is the hearing of the divine books. Let your gift be male; lay your hand on it and cut its throat before the Lord—that is, the bridle of self-control: I bruise my body (1 Corinthians 9:27). Let the sons of Aaron in you—mind and sense—offer the blood. Offer a living victim, holy, pleasing to God (Romans 12:1). Here ends Homily I. Amen.

last_rejected.why: 1 Cor 9:27 says 'I pommel my body and enslave it', not 'I bruise my body'; the Latin 'macero' means 'I mortify/bruise', not Paul's exact wording.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Macero' means 'I bruise/maccerate/mortify'; 'bruise' is within normal range, and citation is correct.

last_rejected.why: iugula means 'slay/kill as sacrifice', not specifically throat-cutting; 'contra Dominum' = 'before the Lord' is rendered but the colon after 'Lord' breaks the syntax, making 'the bridle of self-control' appear as apposition to 'Lord' rather than to the whole sacrificial action.
last_rejected.fix: slay it before the Lord—that is, apply the bridle of self-control: I bruise my body
last_rejected.ruling: iugula = 'cut throat' is standard sacrificial vocabulary; colon punctuation is interpretive, not a meaning-changing error.

last_rejected.why: The Latin first-person 'macero corpus meum' is Paul's words in 1 Cor 9:27, but the English presents it without quotation marks or clear attribution as if Origen speaks, though Paul is the cited authority per work brief.
last_rejected.fix: as Paul says, 'I bruise my body' (1 Corinthians 9:27)
last_rejected.ruling: Parenthetical scripture reference (1 Cor 9:27) already attributes macero corpus meum to Paul; quotation marks are stylistic preference.
